summary: This informational memo lists requirements for Layer 3 provider-provisioned virtual private networks, written from the perspective of the service provider. It applies to many different approaches a provider might use and is meant to guide the design of solutions.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4031 sets out requirements for provider-provisioned Layer 3 VPNs. It gives customers and providers a checklist for describing a service, while leaving the technical design to separate documents.

subtitle: A checklist for evaluating Layer 3 VPN services from customer and provider perspectives.

tldr.problem: Service providers can provision Layer 3 VPNs through different approaches, and a shared checklist is needed to describe how well an approach meets customer and provider needs.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines terms and lists common, customer, provider-network, and management requirements for several Layer 3 VPN approaches.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational checklist for describing an approach, not a comparison of approaches or a specification of how to build a VPN.

facts.label: Routing protocols named
facts.value: Static, RIP, OSPF, IS-IS, and BGP

today: RFC 4031 is an Informational RFC published in April 2005. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it complements the generic requirements in RFC 3809.

sections.title: Scope and Evaluation Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 4031 describes requirements for Layer 3 Provider Provisioned Virtual Private Networks (PPVPNs). It covers network-based, or PE-based, approaches and provider-provisioned CE-based approaches. Requirements common to Layer 2 and Layer 3 VPNs are addressed in RFC 3809.

The RFC is intended as a checklist for documenting how an approach meets each requirement. It does not compare approaches or specify the technical means of providing an L3VPN. It considers four settings: Internet-wide, one provider and one autonomous system, one provider and multiple autonomous systems, and cooperating providers.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC gives a common checklist for describing Layer 3 VPN approaches. It covers several provider arrangements but does not choose a design or rank the approaches.

sections.title: Sites, VPNs, and Network Devices
sections.content:
A site is a set of users that can reach one another using IP without relying on the provider network. An intranet connects sites controlled by one customer; an extranet allows communication between specified sites belonging to different customers.

A Customer Edge (CE) device faces users at a customer site. A Provider Edge (PE) device connects customer equipment to the provider network. A Provider (P) device connects PE devices or other P devices and does not keep VPN state.
sections.plainLanguage: A VPN connects sites that are allowed to communicate. CE devices connect customer sites to the provider; PE devices sit at the provider's edge, while P devices carry traffic inside its network.

sections.title: Tunnels in PE-Based and CE-Based VPNs
sections.content:
A tunnel carries a packet inside another packet format across the provider network. The RFC names GRE, IPsec, IP-in-IP, and MPLS as examples. A hierarchical tunnel carries one tunnel inside another.

In a PE-based L3VPN, a PE has a Virtual Forwarding Instance (VFI) for each VPN it serves. The VFI holds routing and forwarding information for that VPN and terminates tunnels to other VFIs. In a CE-based L3VPN, tunnels typically end at pairs of CEs; the PE does not know which VPN each CE belongs to, and VPN functions are configured on the CEs.
sections.plainLanguage: Both approaches carry customer packets through tunnels. In a PE-based design, the provider edge keeps VPN-specific routing information; in a CE-based design, the customer-edge devices handle the VPN functions.

sections.title: Common, Customer, and Provider Needs
sections.content:
Requirements shared by customers and providers include isolating routing information and traffic between VPNs, supporting IPv4 and IPv6, and supporting quality-of-service modes. The RFC says best-effort service must be supported for all L3VPN types.

Customers need control over intranet and extranet membership, support for different addressing arrangements, and routing-protocol choices. Providers need to scale and manage VPNs, distribute VPN information only where needed, and support inter-provider operation. The document also covers access, tunneling, migration, protection, and interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: Customers need control over who can communicate and how traffic is treated. Providers need to keep VPNs isolated, manageable, and scalable across different networks.

sections.title: Managing and Monitoring the Service
sections.content:
A provider must be able to view the topology, operating state, and order status of each customer's VPN, as well as the equipment that supports it. The RFC recommends standards-based management interfaces wherever feasible.

The management requirements cover fault, configuration, accounting, performance, and security functions. They include checking reachability within a VPN, configuring VPN components consistently, measuring service-level objectives, and reporting faults and performance.
sections.plainLanguage: Providers need tools to configure, monitor, and troubleshoot VPNs. They must be able to check connectivity and measure whether the service meets its stated objectives.

sections.title: Security and Isolation
sections.content:
The RFC treats traffic and routing isolation separately from traditional security properties such as confidentiality, integrity, and authentication. VPN solutions must restrict traffic and routing information to authorized sites.

Where a VPN crosses an untrusted network, the RFC calls for configurable security methods such as IPsec to provide confidentiality, integrity, authentication, and replay protection. Network elements must authenticate peers before providing a service, and solutions must describe how they address relevant threat scenarios.
sections.plainLanguage: VPNs need to keep each customer's traffic and routing information separate. When traffic crosses an untrusted network, the design must explain how it authenticates peers and protects data.
